# Community Bank And Trust - West Georgia (cert 25796)

*Hindsight: failed 2026-05-01. Canary flagged it 4 quarters ahead.*
*After the test window: not part of the reported 2016-2024 results.*

## Summary

As of 2026-03-31, Community Bank And Trust - West Georgia, a bank based in GA with $292.6 million in total assets, ranked 2 out of 4,353 banks on Canary's risk score, placing it in the 100.0th percentile, where higher means riskier. Its capital cushion (the owners' own money that absorbs losses) was nearly gone, with equity at 1.3% of assets against a national median of 10.4%. Problem loans, loan-loss charges and operating losses were all far above typical levels, and the bank was on Canary's watchlist, which covers about 2% of banks.

## Warning signs in the data

Capital was extremely thin: equity was 1.3% of assets, against a national median of 10.4%. The leverage ratio (core capital as a share of average assets) was 0.2% against a median of 10.9%, and the Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio (top-quality capital weighed against the riskiness of assets) was 0.2% against 14.5%. The total risk-based capital ratio, a broader version of that cushion, was 1.5% against a median of 15.7%.

Credit quality was very weak: loans 90+ days past due or no longer accruing interest were 17.3% of loans, against a national median of 0.5%, and loans 30-89 days past due were 5.5% of assets against 0.3%. The Texas ratio, which sets troubled assets against capital plus reserves, was 280.0%, far above the median of 2.9%. Net loan write-offs (loans recorded as lost) ran at 6.3% of loans and provisions for loan losses (money set aside for expected bad loans) at 8.7% of assets, while the national medians for both were 0.0%. These charges drove heavy losses: return on assets was -6.9% against a median of 1.2%, and return on equity was -191.5% against 11.2%. Commercial real estate loans made up 34.5% of loans, above the median of 23.6%, and the code-written concentration section finds the bank crossed both regulatory screening lines for construction and total commercial real estate lending.

Funding points the other way and looked steadier than typical: uninsured deposits were only 3.6% of deposits against a median of 24.4%, core deposits were 91.3% of assets against 75.8%, and cash was 16.2% of assets against 6.9%. Deposits had grown quickly, by 42.6% over the past four quarters against a median of 4.0%, and brokered deposits (money placed through middlemen) were 1.7% of deposits against a median of 0.0%. Losses on bonds available for sale (bonds the bank could sell) stood at -177.9% of equity, far below the national median of 5.8%, a reading made extreme by how small the bank's equity had become.

## Understanding the score

As of 2026-03-31, the bank ranked 2 out of 4,353 banks, in the 100.0th percentile on a scale where higher means riskier. It was flagged on the watchlist, one of 88 banks that quarter, which is the top 2% of scores.

The five features that pushed the score up most were the Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio at 0.2%, contributing +1.741, and return on equity at -191.5%, contributing +1.318. Next came the Texas ratio at 280.0%, contributing +1.050, loans 90+ days past due or not accruing interest at 17.3% of loans, contributing +0.770, and the total risk-based capital ratio at 1.5%, contributing +0.510.

The five features that pulled the score down most were losses on bonds available for sale at -177.9% of equity, contributing -0.273, and asset growth over the past four quarters at 23.9%, contributing -0.219. The others were construction loans at 8.1% of loans, contributing -0.179, total assets of $292.6 million, contributing -0.160, and the efficiency ratio (operating costs as a share of revenue) at 92.4%, contributing -0.129. These downward pulls were small next to the upward ones.

The score ranks banks against each other; it is not a probability of failure, because the model was trained with extra weight on banks that failed.

**What the model can't see.** FDIC data has no loan fair values, no depositor identity, and no non-financial causes such as fraud or management, so the model cannot see them.

## How its ratios moved

As of 2026-03-31, the model ranked this bank 2 out of 4,353 banks, which places it in the 100.0th percentile, where higher means riskier. A year earlier, on 2025-03-31, it was also at the 100.0th percentile, so the model rated the bank about the same as a year earlier. Of the 30 ratios compared with the bank's own history, 15 sat outside their prior range, meaning the span of values over the prior 12 quarters.

Return on equity (profit as a share of the owners' stake) was -191.5%, far below its prior range of 0.4% to 19.1%, and it added +1.318 model log-odds units, which pushed the score up. Return on assets (profit as a share of everything the bank owns) was -6.9%, below its prior range of 0.0% to 0.7%, and it added +0.166 units, which pushed the score up. The leverage ratio (core capital, the bank's own cushion, as a share of average assets) fell -6.5 pp in one quarter to 0.2%, below its prior range of 5.1% to 9.8%, and it added +0.180 units, which pushed the score up.

The provision for loan losses (money set aside for expected bad loans) ran at 8.7% of assets, above its prior range of 0.3% to 1.7%, and it added +0.144 units, which pushed the score up. Net interest margin (the spread earned on lending and investing) was 2.4%, below its prior range of 4.7% to 6.3%, and it added +0.094 units, which pushed the score up. Net loan write-offs (loans recorded as lost, minus recoveries) reached 6.3% of loans, above their prior range of 0.0% to 2.6%, yet at -0.005 units the model gave this ratio little effect on the score despite it being outside its range.

## Compared with similar banks

The FDIC's specialty group for this bank at 2026-03-31: Commercial Lending Specialization.

Peers: 1457 banks in the same specialty group and size tier ($100 million to $1 billion).

As of 2026-03-31, the bank ranked number 2 of 4,353 banks nationally on Canary's score, placing it in the 100.0th percentile, where higher means a higher score. Its weakest ratios stand out both nationally and against similar banks.

The Texas ratio, which compares troubled assets with capital plus reserves, was 280.0%, at the 100.0th percentile nationally, which is unusually high, and at the 100.0th percentile among peers against a peer median of 3.0%, unusually high among its peers too. The total risk-based capital ratio, a measure of the bank's loss-absorbing cushion weighed against the kinds of assets it holds, was 1.5%, at the 0.0th percentile nationally, which is unusually low, and at the 0.1st percentile among peers against a peer median of 15.3%, unusually low among its peers too. The Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio, which counts only the highest-quality capital, was 0.2%, at the 0.0th percentile nationally, which is unusually low, and at the 0.1st percentile among peers against a peer median of 14.2%, unusually low among its peers too. Losses on bonds available for sale (bonds the bank could sell), as a share of equity, came to -177.9%, at the 0.0th percentile nationally, which is unusually low, and at the 0.0th percentile among peers against a peer median of 5.6%, unusually low among its peers too. Return on equity, or profit as a share of the owners' stake, was -191.5%, at the 0.1st percentile nationally, which is unusually low, and at the 0.0th percentile among peers against a peer median of 11.4%, unusually low among its peers too.

Nonaccrual assets (loans no longer earning interest) plus foreclosed property made up 9.2% of assets, at the 99.9th percentile nationally, which is unusually high, and at the 99.8th percentile among peers against a peer median of 0.3%, unusually high among its peers too. ## Real-estate concentration (2006 regulator thresholds)

This section checks a different, more common way banks have failed than SVB's: heavy lending tied to commercial real estate. It applies the screens the OCC, Federal Reserve and FDIC set in 2006 to flag a bank for closer supervisory review; they are not lending limits.

Capital measure: Tier 1 capital plus the loan-loss allowance, which the regulators have used for concentration ratios since March 31, 2020 (FDIC FIL-31-2020; Federal Reserve SR 20-8). The 2006 thresholds were not restated for this measure.

| Test | Bank | Line | Meets it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Construction and land loans ÷ capital | 181.9% | 100% or more | yes |
| Total commercial real estate loans ÷ capital | 319.3% | 300% or more | yes |
| Growth in commercial real estate loans over the prior 36 months | 128.6% | 50% or more | yes |

It crossed both lines: construction loans and total commercial real estate loans.

Total commercial real estate here means construction and land, multifamily, and non-owner-occupied commercial property loans, plus loans to finance commercial real estate not secured by real estate (FDIC call report data).

Crossing a line is a supervisory screen, not a prediction: it has not been tested as a warning signal in Canary.

## How early Canary caught it

With hindsight, the bank failed on 2026-05-01. Canary first flagged it in the quarter ending 2025-06-30, a lead time of 4 quarters before the failure.

At that first flag, the top drivers were the Texas ratio at 158.3%, the Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio at 5.6%, and loans 90+ days past due or not accruing interest at 14.7% of loans. By 2026-03-31 those same measures had worsened further, to 280.0%, 0.2% and 17.3% respectively.

*After the test window: not part of the reported 2016-2024 results.*

## What happened next

In hindsight, the last quarter the bank reported was 2026-03-31, the same quarter this memo covers. The bank failed on 2026-05-01, so there are no later ranks or flags. Our data alone do not distinguish a merger from a closure when a bank stops reporting, but here the recorded failure date settles it.
